slides.title: What CORS is for
slides.summary: CORS lets a server say which other origins may read its responses. It relaxes the same-origin policy; it doesn't add protection.
body: By default, the same-origin policy stops app.example.com from reading a fetch response from api.example.com. CORS lets the API opt in with response headers.

ul: The browser sends an Origin header with the request.
If it matches, the browser gives the response to your JavaScript. If not, the request may still have reached the server, but your code can't read the result.

body: <mark>CORS is enforced by the browser to protect users. It doesn't protect your API from curl, scripts or other servers.</mark>

body.note: A same-origin setup avoids CORS entirely: serve the API under the app's origin (e.g. /api through a reverse proxy or BFF).

rows.head: GET, HEAD, or POST with form content types and simple headers

cells.text: Sends it, then checks the response headers

rows.head: PUT / DELETE / PATCH, JSON body, custom headers

cells.text: Needs an exact origin and Allow-Credentials: true

slides.title: Preflight requests
slides.summary: For non-simple requests, the browser asks with OPTIONS before sending the real request.
body: A preflight is an OPTIONS request describing the real one. The server answers with what it allows, and the browser sends the real request only if it fits.
Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache the answer, saving a round trip on later requests. Browsers cap it (Chrome at 2 hours).
<mark>If a request works in curl but fails in the browser with a CORS error, look at the preflight response in DevTools first.</mark>

figure.alt: A sequence diagram with three lifelines: your JavaScript on app.example, the browser, and api.example. 1: your code calls fetch with method PUT and a JSON body. 2: the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight with Origin https://app.example and Access-Control-Request-Method PUT. 3: the API replies 204 with Access-Control-Allow-Origin https://app.example, Allow-Methods PUT and Max-Age 600. 4: the browser sends the real PUT. 5: the API replies 200 with Access-Control-Allow-Origin again. 6: the browser hands the response to your code. If step 3 or 5 lacks the right headers, the browser blocks your code from reading the response.

slides.title: CORS mistakes
slides.summary: Reflecting any origin with credentials hands your users' data to every website.

ul: Reflecting the Origin header back with Allow-Credentials: true lets any site read logged-in users' data. Check against an exact allowlist.
Allowing null: sandboxed iframes and local files send Origin: null, so attackers can too.
Forgetting Vary: Origin when the header changes per origin, so caches serve one origin's answer to another.

body: <mark>Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is fine for truly public data, and browsers never send cookies with it.</mark>

body.text: No. A simple cross-origin POST is still sent; CORS only hides the response.
Chrome's earlier plan to add CORS preflights for requests to local networks (Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network) was replaced by the Local Network Access permission prompt in Chrome 142.
